title: Which way does your bow lie?
hook: Which wrap pattern tends to hold better?

knows: Everyday objects have sizes, positions and amounts
doesNotKnow: Opposing knot stages make the balanced slipped reef bow sit across the shoe. The granny bow tends to turn along it; impact and moving lace ends can work a bow loose.

misconception: The two pictured methods are interchangeable without checking their mechanism or constraints.
objective: Opposing knot stages make the balanced slipped reef bow sit across the shoe. The granny bow tends to turn along it; impact and moving lace ends can work a bow loose.

claims.text: Opposing knot stages make the balanced slipped reef bow sit across the shoe. The granny bow tends to turn along it; impact and moving lace ends can work a bow loose.
claims.source: Ian Fieggen, Granny Knot Info, https://www.fieggen.com/shoelace/grannyknot.htm (opened 2026-10-14), balanced/opposing stages and bow orientation; Daily-Diamond, Gregg & O'Reilly 2017, doi:10.1098/rspa.2016.0770, full paper opened at https://escholarship.org/content/qt7qs984k7/qt7qs984k7_noSplash_66a8485e2a04a2d12bd2baeb463325cf.pdf. The model step decrements are illustrative, not data.

claims.text: Both can fail. The schematic is not a tying tutorial; loop loss is illustrative, not measured walking data.
claims.source: Scope limits and illustrative assumptions of this card; Illustrative remaining loop=20−steps×rate mm, clipped at 0; matching rate=0.8, opposing=0.3. No claimed empirical lifetime. FC LH-1 (session 2, received by message): verified; see company/reviews/lifehacks-200/fact-check-LH1-2026-10-14.md.

claims.text: Both illustrative loops start at 20 mm at step 0. Changing the second wrap changes its geometry and model loss rate without advancing steps. Walk 20 steps advances from 0 to 20: remaining loop = max(0, 20 − steps × rate) mm, with matching rate 0.8 and opposing rate 0.3. The displayed results are 4 mm and 14 mm. No empirical lifetime is claimed.
claims.source: Computed in src/lib/lifehacks/home-models.ts and src/components/lifehacks/HomeLesson.tsx: 20 − 20 × 0.8 = 4 mm; 20 − 20 × 0.3 = 14 mm. The zero-step initial value is in src/lib/lifehacks/home-lessons.ts. Rates are illustrative coefficients, not measurements. FC LH-1 (session 2, received by message): verified; see company/reviews/lifehacks-200/fact-check-LH1-2026-10-14.md.

claims.text: Which wrap pattern tends to hold better?
claims.source: Chosen comparison question; the prediction refers to the stated default values and selected methods. FC LH-1 (session 2, received by message): verified; see company/reviews/lifehacks-200/fact-check-LH1-2026-10-14.md.

claims.text: A bow lying along the shoe is the sign of matching stages. Making the second stage right-over-left opposes the first and gives the balanced bow that tends to sit across the shoe. It can still fail; the drawing is not a tying tutorial.
claims.source: Ian Fieggen, Granny Knot Info, https://www.fieggen.com/shoelace/grannyknot.htm (opened 2026-10-14), balanced/opposing stages and bow orientation; Daily-Diamond, Gregg & O'Reilly 2017, doi:10.1098/rspa.2016.0770, full paper opened at https://escholarship.org/content/qt7qs984k7/qt7qs984k7_noSplash_66a8485e2a04a2d12bd2baeb463325cf.pdf. The model step decrements are illustrative, not data. Scenario values in the recall question are stipulated. Recall patch by learning-designer (session 2, 2026-10-14), applied by session 1.

recall.question: Both stages of your knot are left-over-right, and the finished bow points along the shoe. What does the lesson suggest changing?
options: Pull both stages as tight as they will go
recall.why: A bow lying along the shoe is the sign of matching stages. Making the second stage right-over-left opposes the first and gives the balanced bow that tends to sit across the shoe. It can still fail; the drawing is not a tying tutorial.
